definition: Holistic means considering something as a whole interconnected system rather than analyzing or treating its parts separately.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word holistic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know holistic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The clinic took a holistic view of health, asking about the patient's sleep, stress, diet, and relationships instead of examining the sore knee alone.
A broad review touches many separate areas, while a holistic one treats those areas as parts of a single connected system.
Holistic thinking connects the parts of one system, but an all-encompassing plan tries to fold in everything around that system as well.

Integrated means combined so the parts work as one connected whole — an integrated transit system where trains and buses share one schedule. Holistic describes a way of looking rather than a way of building: it considers a thing as one interconnected system instead of analyzing the parts separately. Engineers integrate parts; a holistic review treats them as inseparable.

Big-picture means focused on the whole situation rather than the details — a big-picture thinker skips the fine print. Holistic keeps the details in: it insists the parts be studied together as one connected system, not skipped. A big-picture summary may ignore the parts; a holistic assessment connects every one of them.

Holistic means considering something as a whole interconnected system rather than analyzing or treating its parts separately.
Frustrated by downtown gridlock, a city first tried simply widening its busiest road, and traffic got worse as more drivers poured in.
A new planning team then took a holistic approach: they studied bus routes, bike lanes, school start times, parking prices, and housing locations together, because each one affected all the others.
By staggering school schedules and improving two bus lines, they eased the congestion without pouring a single new lane of concrete.
The planners treated traffic as one interconnected system of schedules, transit, and housing rather than fixing one road in isolation, which is exactly what a holistic approach means.

For decades the academy ranked applicants by a single number: the entrance-exam score.
Five years ago it switched to what the admissions office calls a holistic review.
Readers still see the score, but they read it alongside essays, teacher letters, and a record of how the student spent afternoons and summers.
No item is judged alone; a dip in grades is weighed against a semester spent caring for a sick parent.
The office insists the goal is not to lower standards but to see how the pieces of one life explain each other.
